description: We are a team of engineering students passionate about technology, innovation, and space exploration. For NASA Space Apps 2026, we aim to transform NASA Earth observation data into meaningful environmental insights using Python, data analysis, statistics, and AI. We are looking for motivated teammates interested in software development, machine learning, data science, Earth science, and creative problem-solving. Let's explore, innovate, and build something impactful together!
summary: LunaNav answers one question for any landing site on the Moon: if we land here, on this date, will we have power and comms, and for how long? At the lunar south pole the Sun skims the horizon and Earth slips behind the hills, so the same site can be safe on one date and deadly on another. LunaNav traces the real skyline from NASA's LOLA 80 m elevation model, computes where the Sun and Earth sit on it over a full lunar day, and turns that into clear numbers: hours of sunlight, Earth visibility, the longest night and the longest communication gap. Users pick sites from a 26-site catalog or type coordinates, play the lunar day on a timeline, compare up to four sites with a verdict that explains its reasons, and sweep the next 12 landing dates to find the best one. A built-in Luna guide answers plain questions with the site's own numbers. Our Sun and Earth positions match JPL Horizons in 25 of 25 checks, and our sunlight agrees with NASA PGDA illumination maps to within 0.9 percentage points (median, 36 points).
details:
What it does LunaNav is a web app that tells a mission planner, a student or a curious member of the public whether a lunar landing site will have sunlight for solar power and a line of sight to Earth for direct radio, on a chosen landing date and over the following lunar day (29.5 days). It has five screens: Scenarios (pick 2 to 4 sites and dates from a 26-site catalog of Apollo, CLPS and Artemis III candidate regions, or any coordinate), Site view (the real terrain skyline with the Sun and Earth on it, countdowns to sunset, Earthrise or Earthset, and solar irradiance), Timeline (play the whole lunar day; bars show sunlight, Earth visibility and both at once), Compare (side-by-side numbers and a Viable / Marginal / Not viable verdict that always states the reason and the threshold) and Date sweep (the same site on the next 12 landing dates, with the best date highlighted). A built-in Luna guide answers questions such as "Will I have power and comms here?" with the numbers of the site on screen and offers a guided tour.

How it works The astronomy engine computes Sun and Earth directions from the landing site using planetary ephemerides (NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE DE440 kernels, with a built-in analytic model as fallback). The terrain engine reads NASA's LOLA south-pole elevation model (80 m per pixel) and traces the horizon around the site in every direction. Comparing the two gives, hour by hour, whether the Sun's disk and Earth are above the local skyline. A decision layer turns this into sunlight %, Earth visibility %, power-plus-comms %, longest night and longest comms gap, then applies hardware presets (solar + direct radio, relay satellite, RTG / night battery, nuclear + relay) to give a verdict.

Validation Sun and Earth positions agree with JPL Horizons in 25 of 25 comparisons. Average sunlight and Earth visibility agree with NASA PGDA polar illumination maps at 36 test points, with a median difference of 0.9 percentage points for the Sun and 1.2 for Earth.

Benefits and impact The south pole is where Artemis and many commercial landers are going, and there the landing date matters as much as the site: on 10 January 2027 the Shackleton-de Gerlache connecting ridge has sunlight 100 % of the time but sees Earth only 48 % of the time, while Malapert Massif sees Earth all the time but faces a 269-hour (11-day) night. LunaNav makes that trade-off visible in seconds, explains every verdict in plain words, and shows how a launch slip changes the outcome. It is also a teaching tool: anyone can see why the poles are hard.

Tools and languages Python (FastAPI, NumPy, Pydantic, SpiceyPy, rasterio, pytest) for the backend and science engine; TypeScript with React, Vite, Recharts, Zustand and TanStack Query for the web app.

Creativity Instead of a static map, LunaNav puts you on the landing site: you see the real skyline with the Sun and Earth moving over it, and you can scrub through the lunar day. Verdicts are explained rather than given as a black-box score, and the Luna guide lets non-experts ask questions in plain language.

Factors we considered Real terrain shadowing (not a flat horizon), the size of the Sun's disk, libration that moves Earth up and down in the sky, landing-date sensitivity, different spacecraft power and comms hardware, and honest limits: Earth visibility is geometric line of sight, not a radio link budget, and the default verdict thresholds are our team's assumptions, not NASA rules.
